-[[ACE-CSR-enable]]
-===== `aceenable`
-
-`aceenable` is a single-bit CSR.
-(((CSR,aceenable)))
-
-Enabling ACE in any mode is done by writing a 1 to `aceenable`.
-Disabling ACE is done by writing a zero to `aceenable`, which also clears the CCs, as described in <<ACE-tracking-cc-dirtiness>>. When ACE is disabled, any ACE operation will cause an invalid instruction exception, except feature enablement.
-
-[NOTE]
-====
-While the standard floating-point and vector extensions do not support User Mode disable/enable instructions, the ACE unit can in general be enabled and disabled in zUser Mode, instead of using an OS call or trapping.
-However, if the ACE unit contains state from a different process, and its interface is disabled for the current one, enabling it will trap to the Supervisor (as described in <<ACE-ACES-field>>) to allow the latter to first save the state in case it was not saved before and then clear it (lazy context switch).
-
-When a process that has ACE enabled is preempted, the parent modes inherit the state to be able to export and
-re-import the CCs. Hence, `aceenable` is not cleared, and the `*status.ACES` fields (see <<ACE-ACES-field>>) of the parent domains will take the value Enabled.
-Tracking the CCs which are active, resp., dirty is done on an individual basis and is described in <<ACE-tracking-cc-dirtiness>>.
-====
-
-[quote]
-____
-In the "standard" RISC-V way, higher privilege software should be able to look at just sstatus.ACES to know whether to proceed and look at acedirty and possibly save some context.
-The following shows how aceenable accesses can be translated to sstatus.ACES accesses, avoiding the need to context switch aceenable CSR, because it can be interpreted as a virtual interface for sstatus.ACES.
-
-csrrw one, aceenable, a0 does, depending on on state of sstatus.ACES
-
-* ACES=disabled-clean -> ACES=enabled, a0=0
-* ACES=disabled-dirty -> trap
-* ACES=enabled -> a0=1
-
-csrrw zero, aceenable, a0 does
-
-* ACES=disabled-clean -> a0=0
-* ACES=disabled-dirty -> trap
-* ACES=enabled -> clear all CCs, ACES=disabled-clean, a0=1
-
-(The current specification doesn't say anything about transition to ACES=enabled,
-which would allow dirty state with ACES=disabled-clean.)
-
-The rules get a more complex in virtual (V=1) mode,
-where a single write to aceenable can modify both mstatus and vsstatus:
-
-* mstatus.ACES=disabled-dirty -> CSR accesses trigger virtual-instruction trap
-* vsstatus.ACES=disabled-dirty -> CSR accesses trigger illegal-instruction trap
-* otherwise -> result based on previous value of vsstatus
-** write 1: mstatus.ACES and vsstatus.ACES = enabled
-** write 0: mstatus.ACES and vsstatus.ACES = disabled-clean, clear all CCs if any were enabled
-
-(Maybe turn the interface to instructions? We do not need return values.)
-____

-The Disabled-Clean and Disabled-Clobbered states are set by the parent mode.
-Disabled-Clobbered is used when the parent-mode software stack does not save Cryptographic Contexts before transferring control to a process that does not (yet) have enabled ACE. If that process later enables ACE by writing to `aceenable`, the hart traps to the parent mode, allowing lazy context save; the parent must then manually reset all Cryptographic Contexts. In contrast, a software stack that always saves the contexts of a switched-out process must configure only the Disabled-Clean state.
-// The Disabled-Clobbered state is primarily intended for small devices where thread migration between harts is infrequent, and possibly only one process may be dealing with cryptographic operations.
+Attempts to execute any ACE instruction, or to access the ACE CSRs, raise an
+illegal-instruction exception when mstatus.ACES is set to Off.
+
+// TODO: this is potentially suboptimal behavior for H, which might have
+// preferred a virtual-instruction to facilitate lazy context switching when
+// mstatus=off, vsstatus!=off, but it is consistent with FS/VS like this:
+When V=1, both vsstatus.ACES and mstatus.ACES are in effect: attempts to
+execute any ACE instruction, or to access the ACE CSRs, raise an
+illegal-instruction exception when either field is set to Off.

+When mstatus.ACES is set to Initial or Clean, executing any instruction, except
+`ace.reset`, that changes ACE state, including the ACE CSRs, will change
+mstatus.ACES to Dirty.

+When V=1 and neither vsstatus.ACES nor mstatus.ACES is set to Off, executing

+[[ACE-instruction-reset]]
+==== ace.reset
+
+`ace.reset`
+
+Encoding::
+[wavedrom, , svg]
+....
+{reg:[
+    { bits:  7, name: 0x27, attr: ['custom-1'] },
+    { bits:  5, name: 0x0 },
+    { bits:  3, name: 0x7, attr: ['ace.clear'] },
+    { bits:  5, name: 0x0 },
+    { bits: 12, name: 0x0 },
+]}
+....
+
+Description::
+Upon execution of `ace.reset`:
+* `mstatus.ACES=Initial`
+* `vsstatus.ACES=Initial` if executed in VS or VU mode
+* `aceccdirty=0`
+* `aceccactive=0`
+* `acecclazy=0`
+
+TODO: rework aceccdirty, aceccactive, acecclazy
+
+NOTE: `ace.reset` allows optimization of context switches, since higher
+privileges do not have to save the Initial state, nor rely on the Off state to
+perform lazy context switches upon a trap.
+The main benefit would be for programs that have long periods when the ACE unit
+is not reused again.
